subject: Cooking
title: Sound and Crunch: The Forgotten Flavor
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Sound and Crunch: The Forgotten Flavor.

hook.text: Pringles invested millions to engineer the perfect crunch sound. They knew sound sells chips.

buildup.text: Oxford researcher Charles Spence proved that louder crunch sounds make people rate chips as 15% fresher.

discovery.text: The auditory cortex contributes to flavor perception. Silence actually makes food taste stale.

twist.text: Airline food tastes bland partly because engine noise at 85 decibels suppresses taste perception by 30%.

climax.text: Some restaurants now design 'sonic seasoning' — playlists that enhance specific flavors in their dishes.

punchline.text: Crunch isn't texture. It's a flavor you hear.

quiz.question: How does loud background noise affect taste perception?

details.summary: Sound contributes more to flavor perception than most people realize. The crunch of a chip accounts for up to 15 percent of its perceived freshness. Restaurants that manipulate ambient sound can alter how diners perceive sweetness, bitterness, and even texture of food.
details.whyItMatters: Sound is the forgotten sense in eating. Food companies now engineer crunch acoustics, and restaurants design soundscapes to enhance flavor perception, making this an invisible influence on enjoyment.
takeaways: Crunch sounds account for up to 15 percent of perceived freshness
High-pitched ambient sound enhances sweetness perception
Airplane cabin noise suppresses sweet and salty taste sensitivity

faq.question: How do food companies engineer crunch sounds?
faq.answer: Pringles and other chip companies study the acoustic frequency of breaking chips to optimize crunch appeal. Higher-pitched crunches are perceived as fresher. Coating, thickness, and moisture content are adjusted to produce specific sound profiles that consumers associate with quality and freshness.

faq.question: Why does airplane food taste bland?
faq.answer: Cabin pressure and low humidity reduce taste sensitivity by 20 to 30 percent. Additionally, engine noise at 85 decibels specifically suppresses sweet and salty perception while enhancing umami. Airlines now add more umami-rich ingredients to compensate for the acoustic suppression of other tastes.
